extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, biotech industry stakeholders, researchers and policymakers interested in gene-patenting issues
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how the US Supreme Court's Myriad decision and related case law affect patent-eligibility of DNA, cDNA and other biotech inventions, and the practical IP strategies firms should adopt. Focuses on legal standards, jurisdictional differences, and business implications for biotech patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring DNA segments are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: “A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and, as such, cannot be patented.” (Supreme Court holding in Association for Molecular Pathology v Myriad Genetics.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court ruled that isolated human genes that are naturally occurring are not patent-eligible. The decision prompted the USPTO to instruct examiners to reject product claims drawn solely to naturally occurring nucleic acids or fragments, whether isolated or not. The opinion was short and case-specific, and commentators warned it gives limited guidance for other biotech situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA is patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: “Complementary DNA - an artificial product designed to mirror the coding parts of genes - is eligible for patent protection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court upheld patent claims on cDNA on the grounds that cDNA is not naturally occurring: “The lab technician unquestionably creates something new when cDNA is made.” Myriad retained claims covering cDNA, even as claims to isolated genomic DNA were found ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / laws-of-nature exclusion (subject-matter test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal doctrine that 'The laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas have been held not patentable.' (Quoted from Diamond v Chakrabarty context.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foundational exclusion frames subject-matter eligibility inquiries. Diamond v Chakrabarty distinguished a genetically modified microorganism as patentable because it was not merely a product of nature, establishing a precedent that man-made, modified living things can be eligible if they are not natural phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic method claims risk invalidation if directed to natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Prometheus v Mayo: Prometheus' patent claims related to ways of optimizing drug doses were invalid because they relate to a natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prometheus made it harder to obtain patents for diagnostic methods and similar claims that effectively claim natural correlations. The decision influenced how courts and examiners treat method and diagnostic claims in biotech, increasing scrutiny of claims that merely apply natural laws or relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examiner guidance rejecting isolated genomic DNA product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Myriad, the USPTO issued a memo instructing examiners to reject product claims drawn solely to naturally occurring nucleic acids, or fragments of them, whether isolated or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should expect immediate changes at the USPTO in examination practice: product claims to genomic DNA must be re-evaluated, and applicants should consider claim drafting strategies that rely on non-naturally occurring constructs or functional/technical limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO standard: require demonstration of industrial application for gene sequence patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The European Patent Office will grant patents for inventions related to gene sequences as long as applicants can demonstrate the industrial application of the sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the US post-Myriad approach to isolated DNA, the EPO focuses on industrial applicability; applicants should include clear utility and application data in filings to meet EPO standards. This represents a jurisdictional contrast that affects international filing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional differences allow isolated-gene patents in some countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Australia, Canada and Japan allow the patenting of human genes provided they are isolated and the patent application explains how the genes are useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because countries differ on whether isolated genes are patentable, patent-seeking entities must tailor IP strategies by jurisdiction—filing claims and drafting specifications to meet local standards for patent-eligibility and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty about scope of Myriad for other DNA constructs and biological molecules
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many other types of DNA constructs that are patented, such as short nucleotide probes and primers and iRNA constructs; it is unclear whether or how Myriad will be applied to other areas of biotechnology, such as proteins and antibodies, or to other pharmaceutical products isolated from natural sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision drew a bright line between 'naturally occurring DNA' and 'cDNA' but left ambiguity for many synthetic or semi-synthetic constructs; practitioners should expect years of further case law and USPTO/Federal Circuit guidance, and draft claims cautiously to emphasize human-made aspects or technical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business strategy: consider trade secrets where patents are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Now that USPTO examiners will no longer grant patents for isolated genomic DNA, biotech companies are likely to turn to trade secrets to protect their investments and guard valuable data accumulated during research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms should assess risks of reverse engineering and data leakage when shifting to trade secrets, implement appropriate confidentiality measures, and weigh the trade-off between public disclosure (patents) and secrecy (competitive protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio management: revisit, maintain, abandon or renegotiate patent assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that already hold patents over genes will need to revisit their portfolios and consider abandoning patents rather than pay fees to maintain hollow IP rights; businesses that have licensed-in patent rights may want to renegotiate royalty rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-Myriad, firms must audit their holdings, evaluate claim strength under new subject-matter standards, and make economic decisions about maintenance, enforcement, licensing terms, and potential divestment of weakened assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and investment uncertainty from shifting patent-eligibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision could create business uncertainty for a broader range of biotechnology inventions; innovators, competitors, and investors must make important business decisions without knowing whether these types of patents will be upheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders should factor increased legal uncertainty into valuation, R&D investment decisions, and deal-making; consider diversified IP strategies, defensive filings in favorable jurisdictions, and contractual protections for technology transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and political tools remain relevant despite eligibility limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after the decision, patent owners can pursue infringement lawsuits (Myriad sued rivals shortly after the opinion), and political mechanisms (e.g., calls for NIH march-in rights) can be used to influence licensing and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners should not assume loss of all enforcement leverage; litigation, licensing negotiations, and political or regulatory actions can still affect market exclusivity and access. Anticipate mixed legal, commercial, and policy responses following major eligibility rulings.
